The first paragraph works for medieval societies in France, Germany etc. where property rights hadn't been established, but doesn't quite so in Britain and the Netherlands. This is because in countries without property rights you had a communal family unit, where one person (the head of the family) would own everything, "employ" his family members to work on the family business, share out the spare resources amongst the family, and then the next head of the family would own everything.

When Britain and Holland invented property rights, the family wouldn't remain a unit as each child would find employment elsewhere in order to own possessions, land and start their own business, and then when the parents die their possessions are split (not always equally) between their children.

Karl Marx made the same assumption in your first paragraph, which is why he (and his students) was surprised that Britain didn't have a socialist revolution. His base assumption was incorrect, so his conclusions were also incorrect.
